lead: Visual image interpretation is the reading of an image by a trained eye before any software is used. The interpreter pools tone and colour, shape, size, pattern, texture, shadow, site and association to name each object and draw its boundary. It exists because a single pixel or a single band cannot say whether a grey patch is a roof, a dry field or a shadow. It is used to make land-use maps, check crop area, map forests and wetlands, assess flood or fire damage, and update topographic sheets from new imagery.
prereq: You need: map scales and topographic sheets, the spectral signatures and pixel size.

blocks.text: Start with the recorded appearance, then add context. Each element answers a different question about the same target.

items: Tone is the brightness of the target in the recorded band; colour is its hue when three bands are shown. Deep water is dark; dry sand is bright.

Shape is the outline of the object. A rectangular field, a straight canal and a winding river have different shapes. Size is the object's measured length, width or area, read against the image scale; it separates a house from a shed.
Pattern is the arrangement of discrete objects, such as an orchard grid or terrace lines. Texture is the frequency of tone change inside a patch; smooth water and rough canopy differ.
Shadow is the dark area cast by an object. Its direction and length give cues to height and sun position, but it hides the ground inside it.
Site is where the object sits relative to terrain, drainage and transport. Association is what normally lies beside it, such as a car park beside a stadium.

blocks.text: No single element decides a class. A dark rectangle may be a roof or a pond; shape, texture and association settle the name.

An interpretation key is a written or pictorial table that links a land cover to its expected appearance: tone, shape, texture, season and usual neighbours. The interpreter compares the image with the key, then checks doubtful patches in the field.

items: Black-and-white panchromatic image: one broad band, fine detail, no colour.
True colour image: red, green and blue bands shown as red, green and blue. Colour looks natural.
False-colour infrared composite: near-infrared, red and green bands shown as red, green and blue. Healthy vegetation is bright red because it reflects near-infrared strongly.
Thermal image: emitted heat, shown as brightness. Warm roofs and hot sand are bright; it can be taken at night.

blocks.text: Aerial photographs come from aircraft: large scale, high detail, flown on demand, but limited repeat coverage. Satellite images come from fixed orbits: repeated coverage, several spectral bands, usually smaller scale. The two are compared, not ranked.

Season changes the target. A kharif crop field and a rabi crop field look different; a deciduous forest loses leaves. Sun angle changes shadow length and brightness. A low sun gives long shadows and strong relief; a high sun gives short shadows and flatter tone.

Multi-date visual comparison places two or more images of the same area side by side. The interpreter looks for new edges, lost patches and colour or tone changes. Images from the same season are preferred, so that crop stage is not mistaken for real change.
Scale relates a distance on the image to the same distance on the ground. A representative fraction 1:50,000 means one unit on the image represents 50,000 of the same unit on the ground.

blocks.where: S is the scale ratio; d<sub>p</sub> is the photo distance; D<sub>g</sub> is the ground distance in the same unit; M is the denominator of the representative fraction.

blocks.text: At 1:50,000, one centimetre on the image represents 50,000 cm on the ground, which is 500 m. On a vertical photo of flat ground one scale holds everywhere. Over hills the scale changes with ground height, and on a tilted photo it changes across the frame, so measure with a scale found near the object or work on a rectified image.

items: Area scale factor is the square of the linear factor. At 1:50,000, one square centimetre represents 500 m × 500 m = 250,000 m² = 0.25 km².
Multiply a measured photo area by the area represented by one square centimetre to get ground area.

blocks.where: S is the scale of a vertical photo; f is the camera focal length; H is the flying height above datum; h is the ground height above datum; f and H − h in the same unit. Higher ground is closer to the camera, so it appears at a larger scale.

blocks.text: Shadow also gives height. If a shadow is s long on the ground and the sun is at elevation angle e above the horizon, the object is s × tan e high, provided the shadow falls on level ground.

The tower's 1.5 mm shadow gives its height, 25.2 m, as in the second worked example.

spec.aria: A rectangle standing for an aerial photo. Inside: a grid of dots for an orchard, a cluster of round crowns for forest, a dark winding river, a dark oval tank, an oval stadium with small rectangles beside it, and a tower with a long thin shadow. Leader lines name pattern, tone, shape, texture, association and shadow. Below: the shadow 1.5 millimetres at 1 to 20 000 is 30 metres, and with the sun 40 degrees up the tower is 25.2 metres high.

examples.question: An aerial photograph has scale 1:50,000. A forest patch measures 6.4 cm² on the photo. Two field corners are 4.2 cm apart on the same photo. Find the ground distance between the corners and the forest area in km².
steps: Scale 1:50,000 means 1 cm on the photo represents 50,000 cm on the ground.
Convert to metres: 50,000 cm ÷ 100 = 500 m. So 1 cm on the photo represents 500 m on the ground.
Ground distance between the corners = 4.2 cm × 500 m/cm = 2100 m = 2.1 km.
For area, 1 cm² on the photo represents 500 m × 500 m = 250,000 m².
Convert to square kilometres: 250,000 m² ÷ 1,000,000 = 0.25 km² per cm².
examples.answer: The ground distance is 2100 m and the forest area is 1.6 km².
examples.check:
scale = 50000
cm_to_ground = scale / 100.0
distance = 4.2 * cm_to_ground
area = 6.4 * (cm_to_ground ** 2) / 1e6
print(distance)
print(area)

examples.question: A vertical air photo is taken with a 152 mm camera from 3200 m above datum over flat ground at 160 m above datum. (a) Find the photo scale. (b) A tower's shadow is 1.5 mm long on the photo and the sun was 40° above the horizon. Find the shadow length on the ground and the tower's height.
steps: (a) Height of the camera above the ground: H − h = 3200 − 160 = 3040 m.
Scale: S = f ÷ (H − h) = 0.152 m ÷ 3040 m = 1 ÷ 20 000, that is 1:20 000. Both lengths are in metres before dividing.
Check: with the sun at 45° the shadow would equal the height; 40° is a lower sun, so the shadow (30 m) should be longer than the tower (25.2 m), as found.
examples.answer: The scale is 1:20 000, the shadow is 30 m long on the ground and the tower is 25.2 m high.

traps: Shadow is not a dark surface. It hides the ground it falls on, so read the class from the lit side of the object, which faces the sun, or from another date. Shadows always point away from the sun.
Pattern is the arrangement of separate objects; texture is the fine change of tone inside one patch. An examiner may swap the two words.
Area scales as the square of the linear scale. At 1:50,000, 1 cm² is 0.25 km², not 0.5 km².
Season and sun angle can create false change. Two images of the same field may differ because one is kharif and the other is rabi, or because one has long shadows.
The representative fraction has no unit. Convert photo and ground distances to the same unit before dividing, and do not mix centimetres with kilometres.

quiz.q: List six elements used in visual image interpretation.
quiz.a: Tone or colour, shape, size, pattern, texture, shadow, site and association. Any six.

quiz.q: Why can a shadow both help and mislead an interpreter?
quiz.a: Shadow gives a cue to height, shape and sun direction, so it helps identify tall objects. It also hides the ground inside the dark area and can be mistaken for a dark surface such as water or a tar roof.

quiz.q: On a photo at 1:25,000, two corners are 3.6 cm apart and a field measures 5.0 cm². Find the ground distance and the field area.
A field is bright on one date and dark on another. Give two possible causes and say how you would test them.
quiz.a: Causes include crop stage or tillage, soil moisture, and sun angle or season. Check image dates and metadata, compare images from the same season, inspect other bands, and visit the field if possible.
A written or pictorial table that links a land cover to its expected image appearance, such as tone, shape, texture, season and usual neighbours.

quiz.q: Why does healthy vegetation look red in a false-colour infrared composite?
quiz.a: Near-infrared, red and green bands are shown as red, green and blue. Healthy vegetation reflects near-infrared strongly, so the near-infrared band drives the red display colour.

quiz.q: At 1:50,000, a straight canal measures 2.4 cm and a tank measures 3.0 cm². Find the canal length and tank area.
quiz.a: 1 cm = 500 m. Canal length = 2.4 × 500 = 1200 m = 1.2 km. Area: 1 cm² = 0.25 km², so 3.0 cm² = 0.75 km².

beyond: Not for the exam. Operational mapping now uses object-based image analysis, where segments of similar pixels are classified with shape and texture, and deep learning models learn context. Sentinel-2 and Landsat archives support multi-date change detection on cloud platforms, and drones give centimetre-scale photos after floods. Search terms: object-based image analysis, interpretation key, change detection, Sentinel-2 false colour.
